html:
Penicillin is the first antibiotic, a drug made from mould that kills bacteria, discovered by Alexander Fleming in London in 1928. Fleming came back from holiday to find that a mould, Penicillium, had landed on one of his dishes of bacteria and killed the colonies around it.

Fleming could not make enough of the substance to use as a medicine, and the discovery sat mostly unused for ten years. Between 1939 and 1941 a team at Oxford led by Howard Florey and Ernst Chain worked out how to purify it and showed that it cured infections in mice and then in people.

  • Factories in the United States learned to grow the mould in large tanks during the Second World War.
  • By 1944 there was enough to treat Allied soldiers, and after the war it became cheap and common.
  • Fleming, Florey and Chain shared the Nobel Prize in 1945.

Before antibiotics, a scratch, a sore throat or childbirth could end in a fatal infection. Penicillin and the antibiotics that followed it made these mostly curable, and saved many millions of lives. It built on the germ theory of Louis Pasteur and others. Fleming warned early that bacteria could become resistant if the drug was misused, and antibiotic resistance is now a major worry in medicine.
